assessment.nobel_worthiness: Random-coefficients demand estimation with endogenous prices (BLP) and the dynamic-oligopoly framework are core empirical tools. They are used in merger review, antitrust, trade and environmental policy, and are the main way that structural industrial organisation has changed applied work. The contribution is transparent in method and widely reproducible.
assessment.attribution: The BLP demand system (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes 1995) and Berry's inversion are clearly credited to these three. Pakes also has the Ericson-Pakes dynamic framework and the Olley-Pakes production-function approach. Bresnahan, Benkard, Reiss and Levin made important contributions, but a three-person limit forces exclusions.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of use, extensive replication and methodological follow-up. Well past any maturity threshold.
uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats this as an econometric-method prize or as industrial organisation, and who else would belong (Bresnahan, Reiss).
Known sensitivity of BLP estimates to numerical implementation and instrument choice.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Used granular, transparent data to show that household leverage and credit supply expansions drove housing booms, consumption collapses and unemployment in the 2007-09 crisis. The work changed macroeconomic thinking about credit cycles and was built on identification strategies that can be checked directly.
assessment.attribution: The core papers and the 'House of Debt' synthesis are jointly and clearly attributed to Mian and Sufi. Campbell is an important household-finance scholar but is peripheral to this specific discovery.
assessment.maturity: The central results date from 2009-2018 and have been replicated and extended across countries. This is sufficient for recognition, though a longer test of the policy implications would be welcome.
uncertainties: Debate over the relative weight of credit supply versus expectations in housing booms.
Whether the Committee will wait longer after the 2008 crisis literature, and the competing claims of other crisis scholars.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reshaped how economists understand technology and trade as drivers of labour demand, polarisation and local labour-market adjustment. The China-shock work has strong policy relevance and the task framework is now standard.
assessment.attribution: The task approach is shared with Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and others who are not credited here. The China-shock papers are Autor-Dorn-Hanson. Katz is credited mainly for the education-technology race and inequality work. The name set is a compromise, and Dorn is a likely omission.
assessment.maturity: Studies are 10-25 years old and heavily replicated and debated. The maturity is sound.
uncertainties: Robustness of the China-shock estimates to specification and shift-share inference concerns.
Overlap with other recognised work on technology and inequality (Acemoglu, Goldin and Katz), which complicates attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine-learning methods for heterogeneous treatment effects and debiased inference (causal forests, double/debiased ML) have become widespread tools for credible causal inference. They fit the preregistration and design-first agenda because they limit specification search.
assessment.attribution: Double/debiased ML is a many-author contribution (Chernozhukov et al.). Causal forests are Wager-Athey, building on Athey-Imbens. Athey's wider contributions are spread across several areas. Credit is genuinely diffuse, and Wager is the youngest and the most uncertain inclusion.
assessment.maturity: Core papers date from about 2016-2018. Adoption is large, but the long-run track record is shorter than for the older candidates.
uncertainties: The 2021 prize already recognised causal-inference methods, so there may be a perceived overlap.
Diffuse credit and the three-person cap.
Younger work, with less evidence on how well the methods hold up in applications.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Opened up the systematic empirical study of how legal institutions and investor protection shape financial development. It created a large cross-country research programme in finance and law.
assessment.attribution: Credit is concentrated in the LLSV papers. Shleifer has additional contributions in behavioural finance and corporate governance. Vishny is a co-author of much of the corporate-finance work but is left out of this three-name proposal.
assessment.maturity: From the late 1990s and thoroughly tested. Mature, with substantial follow-up and criticism.
uncertainties: Substantial critiques of the legal-origins identification and of the cross-country regression evidence.
Reputational controversy involving Shleifer, which the Committee may weigh differently.
Whether the empirical findings hold up under modern standards for credible inference.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, the Calvo pricing model, the Taylor rule and the Woodford synthesis form the conceptual foundation of modern monetary policy analysis in central banks. The influence on practice is very large.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across many scholars (Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and others). Any three-name selection is arbitrary at the margin. Taylor, Calvo and Woodford map onto the rule, the pricing mechanism and the synthesis.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of use. Some of the framework has been revised after the financial crisis and the inflation episode of 2021-23.
uncertainties: Diffuse credit and the large field of plausible laureates.
Empirical weaknesses of the standard New Keynesian Phillips curve.
Overlap with earlier prizes in macroeconomics and monetary policy.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Built long-run series on top incomes and wealth that restructured the public and scholarly debate on inequality. This is a data-infrastructure achievement with large policy influence.
assessment.attribution: The top-income series are Piketty-Saez (with Atkinson as a deceased collaborator). The offshore-wealth work is Zucman. Saez also has prominent public-finance contributions that overlap with other ballots.
assessment.maturity: The series are over 20 years old. The offshore-wealth and distributional-accounts work is more recent.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over measurement (tax data, imputation, capital-income allocation) and the sensitivity of conclusions to those choices.
Contested theoretical claims about r versus g.
Possible concern over the political salience of the work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification formalises how much can be concluded from data under credible assumptions rather than strong, untestable ones. This matches the aim of honest, transparent inference and the use of bounds in policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the founder of the approach. Tamer made major contributions to incomplete models and moment inequalities. Molinari is an important contributor, but a two- or three-name set involves a judgement call.
assessment.maturity: Manski's foundational work is 30+ years old. The moment-inequality literature is more recent but established.
uncertainties: Applied uptake is narrower than for the point-identification toolkit.
Whether the Committee considers this an econometric theory prize, given earlier econometrics awards.
